# Introduction

A spike-at-zero (SAZ) covariate has a proportion of observations equal
to zero and a continuous distribution of positive values. In `mfp2()`,
setting `spike = TRUE` inside `fp()` models such a covariate with two
components: a binary indicator $I(x = 0)$ and an FP function of the
positive values. The selection procedure then decides which components
to keep.

This vignette shows how to run the analyses in the accompanying paper
([paper reference](#paper-reference)) and how to read the output. For
the model, the selection procedures and the eligibility rules, each
section points to the relevant part of the paper.

Every SAZ fit reports one of four `saz_decision` values (paper,
Section 2.3):

| `saz_decision`        | Retained components                  | Paper notation |
|-----------------------|--------------------------------------|----------------|
| `continuous + binary` | FP function and binary indicator     | $M_{BP}$       |
| `continuous only`     | FP function of positive values only  | $M_P$          |
| `binary only`         | Binary indicator only                | $M_B$          |
| `not selected`        | None (covariate excluded)            | --             |

```{r packages-and-data}
library(mfp2)

data("prostate", package = "mfp2")
```

# Prostate cancer data

The outcome is `lpsa` (log prostate-specific antigen). The SAZ candidate
is `pgg45`, the percentage of Gleason score 4 or 5 (paper, Section 4.1).

```{r prostate-zero-summary}
nrow(prostate)
table(pgg45_zero = prostate$pgg45 == 0)
round(mean(prostate$pgg45 == 0), 2)
length(unique(prostate$pgg45[prostate$pgg45 > 0]))  # distinct positive values
```

The zero proportion (0.36) and the positive proportion (0.64) are both
above the default threshold `min_saz_prop = 0.10`, so `pgg45` is
eligible for SAZ modelling (paper, Section 3.2).

## Univariable analysis with p-values

```{r univariable-saz-fit}
fit_pgg45 <- mfp2(
  lpsa ~ fp(pgg45, df = 4, select = 0.05, alpha = 0.05, spike = TRUE),
  data = prostate,
  family = "gaussian",
  criterion = "pvalue",
  verbose = FALSE
)

print(fit_pgg45, detailed_settings = FALSE, notes = FALSE)
```

What the arguments do (all except `spike` are the defaults):

- `spike = TRUE` requests the SAZ decomposition.
- `df = 4` allows at most an FP2 function for the positive values.
- `select` is the significance level for including the covariate.
- `alpha` is the significance level for choosing the FP function and for
  the tests that remove a component (paper, Sections 2.3.1--2.3.2).
- `detailed_settings = FALSE` and `notes = FALSE` shorten the printed
  output.

The selected model is `binary only`: the FP function is dropped, so
every positive value of `pgg45` gets the same fitted value (paper,
Section 4.2).

`predict()` takes covariates on their original scale and builds the
indicator and FP terms itself:

```{r univariable-saz-predictions}
newdat <- data.frame(pgg45 = c(0, 4, 20, 45, 60, 100))
predict(fit_pgg45, newdata = newdat, type = "link")
```

The prediction is about 1.74 at zero and about 2.90 at every positive
value.

`plot()` returns a list of ggplot objects, one per covariate.
`partial_only = TRUE` plots only the fitted effect, without
partial residuals. A `binary only` effect shows as two points with
confidence intervals. The intervals do not account for model selection.

```{r univariable-saz-plot, fig.cap="Binary-only SAZ model for pgg45 (paper, Figure 1)."}
p1 <- plot(fit_pgg45, terms = "pgg45", partial_only = TRUE)
p1[["pgg45"]]
```

## Forcing inclusion or the full SAZ model

Three settings override parts of the selection (paper, Section 3.1 and
the table of arguments there).

**`select = 1`** keeps `pgg45` in the model. `alpha` still controls the
choice of FP function and the removal of components, so any SAZ
decision except `not selected` can result.

```{r select-one}
fit_forced <- mfp2(
  lpsa ~ fp(pgg45, select = 1, alpha = 0.05, spike = TRUE),
  data = prostate,
  family = gaussian(),
  criterion = "pvalue",
  verbose = FALSE
)
print(fit_forced, detailed_settings = FALSE, notes = FALSE)
```

**`keep`** does the same for any `criterion`. It is an argument of
`mfp2()`, not of `fp()`, and takes variable names. The multivariable
model in the next section excludes `pgg45`; `keep = "pgg45"` keeps it in:

```{r keep}
fit_keep <- mfp2(
  lpsa ~ fp(pgg45, spike = TRUE) + fp(age) +
    fp(cavol) + fp(weight) + fp(bph) + fp(cp) + svi,
  data = prostate,
  family = gaussian(),
  criterion = "pvalue",
  select = 0.05,
  alpha = 0.05,
  keep = "pgg45",
  verbose = FALSE
)
print(fit_keep, detailed_settings = FALSE, notes = FALSE)
```

**`force_max_fp = TRUE`** in `fp()` keeps the binary indicator and the
most complex FP function allowed by `df` (FP2 here). Components are not
removed, whatever the criterion.

```{r force-max-fp}
fit_maxfp <- mfp2(
  lpsa ~ fp(pgg45, spike = TRUE, force_max_fp = TRUE),
  data = prostate,
  family = gaussian(),
  criterion = "pvalue",
  verbose = FALSE
)
print(fit_maxfp, detailed_settings = FALSE, notes = FALSE)
```

## Multivariable analysis

SAZ covariates can be mixed with ordinary FP covariates and with binary
covariates entered without `fp()` (here `svi`). The SAZ decision for
`pgg45` is made in each backfitting cycle, given the current functions
of the other covariates (paper, Section 2.4). Settings passed to
`mfp2()` (`select`, `alpha`) apply to all covariates unless overridden
inside `fp()`.

```{r multivariable-saz-fit}
fit_multi <- mfp2(
  lpsa ~ fp(pgg45, spike = TRUE) + fp(age) +
    fp(cavol) + fp(weight) + fp(bph) + fp(cp) + svi,
  data = prostate,
  family = gaussian(),
  criterion = "pvalue",
  select = 0.05,
  alpha = 0.05,
  verbose = FALSE
)
print(fit_multi, detailed_settings = FALSE, notes = FALSE)
```

After adjustment, `pgg45` is `not selected`. Only `cavol` (log),
`weight` (linear) and `svi` are retained (paper, Section 4.3).

## Selection with AIC or BIC

With `criterion = "aic"` or `"bic"`, all candidate SAZ models are
compared in a single step and `select` and `alpha` are ignored (paper,
Sections 2.3.3 and 4.4).

```{r aic-saz-fit}
fit_pgg45_aic <- mfp2(
  lpsa ~ fp(pgg45, spike = TRUE),
  data = prostate,
  family = "gaussian",
  criterion = "aic",
  verbose = FALSE
)
print(fit_pgg45_aic, detailed_settings = FALSE, notes = FALSE)
```

AIC penalises extra parameters less than the 0.05 p-value test does, and
selects `continuous only` with a log function. There is no binary
indicator. For `pgg45 = 0` the FP term is set to zero (`log(0)` is not
computed), so the prediction at zero is the uncentred intercept. This
equals the fitted log function at `pgg45 = 1`.

```{r aic-saz-predictions}
newdat <- data.frame(pgg45 = c(0, 4, 25, 100))
predict(fit_pgg45_aic, newdata = newdat, type = "link")
```

```{r aic-saz-plot, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Continuous-only SAZ model for pgg45 selected by AIC (paper, Figure 2)."}
p2 <- plot(fit_pgg45_aic, terms = "pgg45", partial_only = TRUE,
           show_grid = TRUE)
p2[["pgg45"]]
```

BIC penalises extra parameters more than AIC does, and selects
`binary only`, the same result as the p-value analysis:

```{r bic-saz-fit}
fit_pgg45_bic <- mfp2(
  lpsa ~ fp(pgg45, spike = TRUE),
  data = prostate,
  family = "gaussian",
  criterion = "bic",
  verbose = FALSE
)
print(fit_pgg45_bic, detailed_settings = FALSE, notes = FALSE)
```

# Simulated data: continuous + binary

The prostate data do not produce `continuous + binary`. Section 4.5 of
the paper therefore simulates data from its Equation 14: an FP2
function with powers (0.5, 1) for positive values, a binary effect
$\gamma = 2$, and about 30% zeros.

```{r simulate-both-components, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(2107)
n <- 5000

is_zero <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.30) == 1
x_saz <- ifelse(is_zero, 0, runif(n, min = 1, max = 12))

# True FP2 function for positive values; 0 at x = 0
positive <- x_saz > 0
f_saz <- numeric(n)
f_saz[positive] <- 4.0 * sqrt(x_saz[positive]) - 0.9 * x_saz[positive]

alpha <- 1.5  # intercept
gamma <- 2.0  # binary-indicator effect
z_saz <- as.numeric(x_saz == 0)
y <- alpha + gamma * z_saz + f_saz + rnorm(n, sd = 1)

dat_bincont <- data.frame(y = y, x_saz = x_saz)
```

`center = FALSE` makes the coefficients directly comparable with the
generating values.

```{r simulated-saz-fit, eval=FALSE}
fit_bincont <- mfp2(
  y ~ fp(x_saz, center = FALSE, spike = TRUE),
  data = dat_bincont,
  family = gaussian(),
  criterion = "pvalue",
  min_saz_prop = 0.10,
  verbose = FALSE
)
print(fit_bincont, detailed_settings = FALSE, notes = FALSE)

predict(fit_bincont, newdata = data.frame(x_saz = c(0, 1, 5, 7, 12)))

p3 <- plot(fit_bincont, terms = "x_saz", partial_only = TRUE,
           show_grid = TRUE)
p3[["x_saz"]]
```

Results reported in the paper:

| Parameter                 | True | Estimate (SE) |
|---------------------------|------|---------------|
| Intercept $\alpha$        | 1.5  | 1.578 (0.212) |
| $x^{0.5}$                 | 4.0  | 3.977 (0.190) |
| $x$                       | -0.9 | -0.904 (0.040)|
| Binary $\gamma$           | 2.0  | 1.930 (0.213) |

The selected model is `continuous + binary` with powers (0.5, 1). The
prediction at zero is $\hat\alpha + \hat\gamma \approx 3.51$. Over the
positive values, the predictions rise to a peak near $x = 5$ and then
fall (paper, Figure 3).

# Several SAZ covariates in one model

Appendix A of the paper simulates three SAZ covariates, one for each
retained decision, plus an ordinary FP covariate (`x4`) and two noise
covariates (`x5`, `x6`). Each SAZ covariate gets its own decision
within the backfitting.

```{r simulate-multiple-saz, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(2107)
n <- 10000
p <- 6
rho <- 0.20
mu <- rep(3, p)
sigma <- 0.60
Sigma <- matrix(rho * sigma^2, nrow = p, ncol = p)
diag(Sigma) <- sigma^2

repeat {
  X <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = n, mu = mu, Sigma = Sigma)
  if (all(X > 0)) break
}
colnames(X) <- paste0("x", 1:6)
x1 <- X[, 1]; x2 <- X[, 2]; x3 <- X[, 3]
x4 <- X[, 4]; x5 <- X[, 5]; x6 <- X[, 6]

# Introduce zeros in the three SAZ covariates
x1[rbinom(n, 1, 0.30) == 1] <- 0
x2[rbinom(n, 1, 0.25) == 1] <- 0
x3[rbinom(n, 1, 0.35) == 1] <- 0

# FP transformation of positive values; 0 at x = 0
positive_fp <- function(x, power) {
  out <- numeric(length(x))
  pos <- x > 0
  out[pos] <- if (power == 0) log(x[pos]) else x[pos]^power
  out
}

# Linear predictor (paper, Equation 15)
eta <- 0.5 +
  20.00 * positive_fp(x1, -2) - 1.40 * (x1 == 0) +   # FP1 + binary
  15.00 * positive_fp(x2, -2) +
   0.25 * positive_fp(x2, 2) +                         # FP2 only
   1.40 * (x3 == 0) +                                  # binary only
   4.00 * log(x4)                                      # ordinary FP1

y <- eta + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.80)
simdat <- data.frame(y, x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6)

colMeans(simdat[c("x1", "x2", "x3")] == 0)  # zero proportions
```

```{r multiple-saz-fit, eval=FALSE}
fit_sim <- mfp2(
  y ~ fp(x1, spike = TRUE, center = FALSE) +
    fp(x2, spike = TRUE, center = FALSE) +
    fp(x3, spike = TRUE, center = FALSE) +
    fp(x4, center = FALSE) +
    fp(x5, center = FALSE) +
    fp(x6, center = FALSE),
  data = simdat,
  family = "gaussian",
  criterion = "bic",
  verbose = FALSE
)
print(fit_sim, detailed_settings = FALSE, notes = FALSE)
```

The paper reports that the true form is selected for every covariate:

| Covariate | `saz_decision`        | Selected function |
|-----------|-----------------------|-------------------|
| `x1`      | `continuous + binary` | FP(-2) + binary   |
| `x2`      | `continuous only`     | FP(-2, 2)         |
| `x3`      | `binary only`         | binary            |
| `x4`      | not SAZ               | FP(0) (log)       |
| `x5`, `x6`| not SAZ               | excluded          |

All estimated coefficients are close to the generating values (paper,
Appendix A). This is one sample, so it does not show how often the
correct model is selected.

# Matrix interface

`mfp2()` also accepts a numeric matrix `x` and a response `y`. SAZ
covariates are then named in `spike_vars` instead of using
`fp(..., spike = TRUE)`. The two interfaces give the same fit (paper,
Appendix B). The code below refits the three prostate models and
compares their coefficients with the formula fits above.

```{r matrix-fits}
y <- prostate$lpsa
x <- as.matrix(prostate[, "pgg45", drop = FALSE])  # drop = FALSE keeps a matrix
x_multi <- as.matrix(
  prostate[, c("pgg45", "age", "cavol", "weight", "bph", "cp", "svi")]
)

fit_pgg45_mat <- mfp2(x, y, family = "gaussian", criterion = "pvalue",
                      select = 0.05, alpha = 0.05, spike_vars = "pgg45",
                      verbose = FALSE)

fit_multi_mat <- mfp2(x_multi, y, family = "gaussian", criterion = "pvalue",
                      select = 0.05, alpha = 0.05, spike_vars = "pgg45",
                      verbose = FALSE)

fit_aic_mat <- mfp2(x, y, family = "gaussian", criterion = "aic",
                    spike_vars = "pgg45", verbose = FALSE)

print(fit_pgg45_mat, detailed_settings = FALSE, notes = FALSE)
```

# Further details

See `?mfp2`, `?fp`, `?predict.mfp2` and `?plot.mfp2` for all
arguments. The paper describes the SAZ model and selection procedures
(Section 2), the software interface, eligibility checks and methods for
fitted objects (Section 3), and discusses the results in more detail
(Section 4 and Appendices A--B).

## Paper reference {#paper-reference}

Kipruto, E., and Sauerbrei, W. *Modelling Spike-at-Zero Covariates with
Fractional Polynomials in R*. Manuscript submitted to the *Journal of
Statistical Software*.
